generatedProse.concept-context: Research often collects sensitive personal data, so the duties of confidentiality, consent and anonymity carry real weight across disciplines. Participants agree to take part on the understanding that their responses are secure and that they cannot be identified in any write-up. Where a study involves children or other vulnerable groups, these duties tighten, and the ethics committee expects to see the extra safeguards.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students who have finished the same set of participant interviews and turn to writing up.

{{learner-a}} quotes participants by name, emails the raw recordings to a collaborator without asking, and keeps the files on a personal laptop. The write-up reads vividly, but consent was never secured for sharing, and named quotations make individuals identifiable. The duties of confidentiality, consent and anonymity have all been missed.

{{learner-b}} secures signed consent before sharing anything, stores the recordings securely, and reports participants as Participant A and Participant B. Where a participant is under eighteen, the extra requirements are checked with the ethics committee first. The data still tells its story, but no one can be identified from it.

Both students gathered the same material. Only {{learner-b}} treated the people behind the data as owed confidentiality, consent and anonymity.
generatedProse.summary: Collecting data brings duties to the people who provide it. You can now apply the duties of confidentiality, consent and anonymity, justify the extra care that children and vulnerable participants require, and appraise how data should be secured, shared and anonymised. The final lesson widens the view to rigour across the whole project.

check.body: Why does research involving children or other vulnerable participants call for additional care?

items.text: Because they may be less able to give fully informed, voluntary consent, so extra safeguards and expert advice are needed.
Because their data is more interesting to examiners.
Because anonymisation is not required for children.
Because consent forms do not apply to anyone under eighteen.

feedback.correct: That's right. Reduced capacity to give informed, voluntary consent means extra safeguards and advice are needed.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Think about capacity to consent, not convenience.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Children and vulnerable participants may be less able to consent fully, so the duties tighten and expert advice is needed; they do not relax.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; carry the cast only through the {{learner-a}} (weaker) and {{learner-b}} (stronger) tokens, never a literal name (the pack supplies the whole body, but not the names). Each example paragraph must begin with its token, weaker first - merge-context.js's wrapProse() only emits the we-weaker/we-stronger cue classes for a paragraph that leads with the token. The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
